subject: Career
title: Power Posing: Myth vs. Reality
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Power Posing: Myth vs. Reality.

hook.text: Amy Cuddy's TED talk said standing like a superhero boosts confidence. Then replication studies failed.

buildup.text: The hormonal claims — more testosterone, less cortisol — didn't hold up in larger studies.

discovery.text: But self-reported confidence did increase. Feeling powerful, even briefly, changes behavior.

twist.text: The mechanism isn't hormones — it's a psychological reset. A ritual that says 'I've got this.'

climax.text: Any pre-interview ritual that builds confidence works. The pose is optional; the mindset isn't.

punchline.text: Fake confidence long enough and the real kind shows up.

quiz.question: What aspect of power posing held up in replication studies?

details.summary: Amy Cuddy's 2012 claim that power posing raises testosterone and lowers cortisol has largely failed to replicate. However, expansive body language before interviews does appear to increase subjective feelings of confidence even if hormonal effects are unproven.
details.whyItMatters: Separating the myth from the reality allows you to use body language strategically without relying on debunked hormonal claims. Feeling confident, even through posture, genuinely improves performance.
takeaways: Hormonal claims of power posing have not been reliably replicated
Expansive postures do increase self-reported confidence
Use open body language during the interview itself for best effect

faq.question: Should you still power pose before an interview even though the science is disputed?
faq.answer: If it makes you feel more confident, there is no harm. The psychological benefit of feeling expansive and taking up space appears real even if the specific hormonal pathway is unproven. Think of it as a confidence ritual rather than a scientific protocol.

faq.question: What body language actually makes a measurable difference during interviews?
faq.answer: Open posture, steady eye contact, genuine smiling, and purposeful hand gestures consistently correlate with higher interviewer ratings. These in-interview behaviors have stronger evidence than any pre-interview posing routine.
